questions.q: Chalk, sand and clay are each made up of a very large number of extremely small basic units. What does the chapter call these units?
questions.a: Constituent particles
o: Constituent particles
Interparticle spaces
Interparticle attractions
Specks of powder

questions.q: At room temperature one substance is a solid and another is a gas. According to the chapter, what mainly decides that they are in different physical states?
questions.a: The strength of the attraction between their constituent particles is different
o: The strength of the attraction between their constituent particles is different
Only the solid is made of constituent particles, not the gas
The particles of the gas are big enough to be seen by the eye
The solid has been ground into a powder, but the gas has not

questions.q:
Assertion (A): No sugar can be seen in a glass of water that has been stirred until the sugar dissolved completely.
Reason (R): When sugar dissolves, it breaks into constituent particles that are too small to be seen even through an ordinary microscope.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

questions.q:
Consider these statements.
I. Each tiny grain of sugar is made up of millions and millions of constituent particles.
II. The strength of the attraction between particles depends only on the distance between them, not on the substance.
III. The strength of the interparticle forces decides the physical state of a substance.
Which of these statements is/are correct?
questions.a: I and III only
o: I and III only
I and II only
II and III only
I, II and III

questions.q: Differentiate between interparticle spaces and interparticle attractions, writing one line about each.
questions.a: Interparticle spaces are the spaces between the particles of a substance (for example, the spaces between water particles that dissolved sugar particles occupy). Interparticle attractions are the attractive forces that hold the constituent particles of matter together.
s: States that interparticle spaces are the spaces between particles
States that interparticle attractions are the attractive forces holding the particles together

questions.q: True or false? 'If the distance between two particles of a substance increases only a little, the attraction between them also becomes only a little weaker.' Give your verdict and the correct idea.
questions.a: False. The chapter says that even a slight increase in the distance between particles decreases the interparticle forces drastically, so a small increase in distance makes the attraction much weaker, not only a little weaker.
s: Gives the verdict: False
Corrects it: even a slight increase in distance decreases the interparticle force drastically

questions.q: Describe a kitchen situation, without using sugar, in which you can tell by taste that a substance is present in water even though you cannot see any of it. Then explain your situation using constituent particles and interparticle spaces.
questions.a: A spoon of common salt is stirred into a glass of water until it dissolves completely; no salt can be seen, but every sip tastes salty. On dissolving, the salt breaks up into its constituent particles, which are too small to be seen. These particles spread through the water and occupy the interparticle spaces between the water particles, so their presence is sensed by taste in every part of the water.
s: Describes a soluble substance (such as common salt or glucose) stirred into water until it dissolves, which can be tasted but not seen
Explains that it breaks into constituent particles too small to be seen
Explains that the particles occupy the spaces between water particles throughout, so they are sensed by taste

questions.q:
Answer briefly.
(a) A piece of chalk is ground into a very fine powder. Is each speck of the powder still chalk?
(b) If the grinding could go on and on, what would we finally reach?
(c) Are grains of sand the smallest units of the rock they came from?
questions.a: (a) Yes. Grinding is a physical change; only the size of each speck becomes smaller and no new substance forms. (b) We would reach tiny units that cannot be broken down any further: the constituent particles of chalk. (c) No. Grains of sand are themselves made up of a large number of constituent particles.
s: (a) Yes, each speck is still chalk; only its size has reduced
(b) The constituent particles, which cannot be broken down further
(c) No, each grain is made of a large number of constituent particles

questions.q:
After a football match in Ranchi, a coach adds two spoons of glucose powder to a bottle of water and shakes it until no powder can be seen. Answer each part in one line.
(a) Will a sip from the top of the bottle now taste sweet?
(b) What has the glucose broken up into?
(c) Where in the water have these particles gone?
(d) Why can the players not see the glucose in the water?
(e) Is one tiny grain of glucose powder a single constituent particle, or many?
questions.a: (a) Yes, it tastes sweet, because the glucose has dissolved and is present all through the water. (b) Into its constituent particles, which cannot be broken down further. (c) They occupy the interparticle spaces between the water particles. (d) The constituent particles are so small that they cannot be seen even through an ordinary microscope. (e) Many: each tiny grain is made up of millions and millions of constituent particles.
s: (a) Yes, the top layer tastes sweet
(b) Into its constituent particles
(c) Into the interparticle spaces between water particles
(d) The particles are too small to be seen even through an ordinary microscope
(e) Many: millions and millions of constituent particles

questions.q:
Three Class 8 students in Dehradun each bring one observation to a class debate on 'Is matter made of particles too small to see?'. Aditi broke a chalk stick into 2 pieces, then into about 30 small pieces, and ground them in a mortar; under a magnifying glass every speck of the powder was still chalk. Bala stirred two teaspoons of sugar into a glass of water until no sugar could be seen, and a spoonful from the top layer tasted sweet. Chetan looked at sand from a riverbank and saw that it is made of many separate grains.
(a) Is Aditi's grinding a physical change or a chemical change? Give the reason.
(b) Where is the sugar in Bala's glass, and why can it not be seen?
(c) Chetan says the sand grains are the smallest units of the rock they came from. Is he right?
(d) Which one of the three observations best shows that matter contains particles too small to see? Justify your choice.
questions.a: (a) A physical change: the chalk does not change into a new substance; only the size of each speck is reduced. (b) The sugar has broken up into its constituent particles, which occupy the spaces between the water particles; they are too small to be seen even through an ordinary microscope. (c) No. Grains of sand are not the smallest units; each grain is made up of a large number of constituent particles. (d) Bala's: it shows the sugar is still present (it can be tasted) even though nothing can be seen. Aditi's specks and Chetan's grains are still visible pieces, so on their own they do not show particles too small to see.
s: (a) Physical change, because no new substance forms and only the size of the specks is reduced
(b) The sugar is present as constituent particles in the spaces between water particles, too small to be seen
(c) No, each sand grain is itself made of a large number of constituent particles
(d) Chooses Bala's observation and justifies it: present by taste but invisible, while the specks and grains can still be seen

questions.q: What is the melting point of a solid?
questions.a: The minimum temperature at which the solid melts to become a liquid at atmospheric pressure
o: The minimum temperature at which the solid melts to become a liquid at atmospheric pressure
The temperature at which a liquid boils and turns into vapour at atmospheric pressure
The temperature at which the particles of the solid first begin to vibrate
The highest temperature the solid can reach before it turns into a powder

questions.q: Meena's kitchen shelf holds a steel ladle, a bottle of mustard oil, a kettle with steam rising from it and a football full of air. In which of these are the particles held in fixed positions, able only to vibrate?
questions.a: The steel ladle
o: The steel ladle
The mustard oil in the bottle
The steam rising from the kettle
The air inside the football

questions.q:
Match each item in Column I with the correct description in Column II.
Column I: 1. Particles of a solid at room temperature; 2. Particles of a solid that is being heated; 3. Particles of a solid at its melting point; 4. A solid with weak interparticle forces.
Column II: A. start leaving their fixed positions; B. has a low melting point; C. vibrate about fixed positions; D. vibrate more vigorously.

Assertion (A): An iron nail has a definite shape and a definite volume.
Reason (R): The particles of a solid are completely still and do not move at all.
questions.a: A is true but R is false.
o: A is true but R is false.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is false but R is true.

questions.q: Give two reasons, in terms of its particles, why a stone has a definite shape and a definite volume.
questions.a: (1) The particles of a stone, like those of any solid, are tightly packed and the interparticle attractions between them are very strong. (2) These strong forces hold the particles in fixed positions; they can only vibrate about their positions and cannot move past each other.
s: Particles are tightly packed with very strong interparticle attraction
Particles are held in fixed positions; they only vibrate and cannot move past each other

questions.q:
A new solid Y melts at 650 °C at atmospheric pressure. The chapter gives these melting points: ice 0 °C, urea 133 °C, iron 1538 °C.
(a) Arrange ice, urea, iron and Y in increasing order of the strength of their interparticle attraction.
(b) A sample of Y is kept at 600 °C. Is it a solid or a liquid? Give the reason.
questions.a: (a) Ice, urea, Y, iron: weak interparticle forces give a low melting point and strong forces give a high one, so the order of melting points (0, 133, 650, 1538 °C) is the order of attraction. (b) Solid: 600 °C is below its melting point of 650 °C, so its particles are still vibrating about fixed positions and have not started to leave them.
s: (a) Ice, urea, Y, iron, from the weakest to the strongest attraction
(b) Solid, because 600 °C is below its melting point of 650 °C

questions.q:
Table 7.1 of the chapter gives these melting points: ice 0 °C, urea 133 °C, iron 1538 °C.
(a) Which of the three solids has the lowest melting point?
(b) Are the interparticle forces in that solid weak or strong compared with the other two?
(c) By how many degrees Celsius is the melting point of urea higher than that of ice?
questions.a: (a) Ice (0 °C). (b) Weak: solids with weak interparticle forces have low melting points. (c) 133 - 0 = 133 degrees Celsius.
s: (a) Ice
(b) Weak, because a low melting point means weak interparticle forces
(c) 133 degrees Celsius

questions.q: Asha says, 'Ice melts at only 0 °C while iron needs 1538 °C, so there must be no attraction at all between the particles of ice.' Check her claim: say what is right in it, what is wrong, and give your verdict.
questions.a: Partly right. Right: a low melting point means weak interparticle forces, so the attraction between ice particles is much weaker than between iron particles. Wrong: below 0 °C ice is a solid with a definite shape and volume, which means its particles are held in fixed positions by attraction; with no attraction at all it could not be a solid. Verdict: the attraction in ice is weaker than in iron, not zero.
s: Right part: the low melting point shows the forces in ice are weaker than in iron
Wrong part: as a solid, ice has a definite shape, so attraction must hold its particles in fixed positions
Verdict: partly right; the attraction is weaker, not absent

questions.q:
An ice cube at -10 °C is taken out of a freezer and warmed slowly at atmospheric pressure until all of it has melted.
(a) What are the particles of the ice doing at -10 °C?
(b) What changes in their motion as the ice warms up towards 0 °C?
(c) What happens to the particles and to the interparticle forces at 0 °C, and what is this temperature called for ice?
(d) For most substances, are the particles in the liquid state closer together or farther apart than in the solid state?
(e) In what way is ice an exception to your answer in (d)?
questions.a: (a) They vibrate (move to and fro) about fixed positions; strong attraction stops them moving past each other. (b) They vibrate more and more vigorously. (c) The vibrations become so vigorous that the particles start leaving their positions; the interparticle forces weaken and the ice turns into liquid water. 0 °C is the melting point of ice. (d) Generally the particles in a liquid are somewhat farther apart than in the solid. (e) In ice the particles are farther apart than in liquid water, which is the opposite of the general case.
s: (a) Vibrate about fixed positions
(b) Vibrate more vigorously as it warms
(c) Particles leave their positions, forces weaken, it becomes liquid; this is the melting point
(d) Farther apart in the liquid, generally
(e) Ice particles are farther apart than those in water

questions.q:
A small casting unit in Rajkot melts a metal M and pours it into moulds. Its notes say that M melts at 660 °C at atmospheric pressure and that the molten metal is poured when it is at 680 °C. Two moulds are available: one made of iron (melting point 1538 °C, as in Table 7.1 of the chapter) and a cheaper one made of a material P that melts at 600 °C. At room temperature, 25 °C, M is a hard block.
(a) Why does the block of M keep its own shape on the workbench at 25 °C?
(b) Compared with ice (melting point 0 °C), is the interparticle attraction in M weaker or stronger? Give the reason.
(c) What would happen to a mould of material P when molten M at 680 °C is poured into it?
(d) Which mould should the unit use? Justify using the melting points.
questions.a: (a) At 25 °C M is a solid: its particles are tightly packed and held in fixed positions by strong interparticle attraction, so they only vibrate and it keeps a definite shape. (b) Stronger: M's melting point (660 °C) is far higher than that of ice, and strong interparticle forces give a high melting point. (c) 680 °C is above P's melting point of 600 °C, so the mould would be heated past its melting point and would start to melt and lose its shape. (d) The iron mould: its melting point, 1538 °C, is far above 680 °C, so it stays solid and keeps its shape, while the cheaper mould would melt.
s: (a) Solid: tightly packed particles held in fixed positions by strong attraction
(b) Stronger, because its melting point is much higher than that of ice
(c) The mould of P would start to melt, since 680 °C is above 600 °C
(d) Chooses the iron mould, because 1538 °C is far above 680 °C

questions.q: Which statement about the particles of a liquid is correct?
questions.a: They can move freely, but only within a limited space
o: They can move freely, but only within a limited space
They are held in fixed positions and can only vibrate
They move freely in all directions and fill the whole container
They have no attraction at all between them

questions.q: Tanvi pours 350 mL of mustard oil from a clean, dry round bottle into a clean, dry square tin. What will she find?
questions.a: The oil takes the square shape of the tin and still measures 350 mL
o: The oil takes the square shape of the tin and still measures 350 mL
The oil keeps the round shape of the bottle and measures 350 mL
The oil takes the square shape of the tin and spreads to more than 350 mL
The oil keeps the round shape of the bottle but measures less than 350 mL

questions.q: Nimmi says liquids should be grouped with solids because both have a definite volume. Which fact from the chapter best shows a key difference between the two states?
questions.a: A liquid takes the shape of its container, but a solid keeps its own shape
o: A liquid takes the shape of its container, but a solid keeps its own shape
A solid has a definite volume, but a liquid does not
The particles of a liquid move freely in all directions to fill any space
The particles of a solid do not vibrate, but those of a liquid do

questions.q:
Consider these statements about liquids.
I. Liquids flow because there is no attraction at all between their particles.
II. If water is poured out of a container whose walls are not clean, the level in the next container may be slightly less, because some water sticks to the walls.
III. The boiling point is the temperature at which a liquid boils and turns into vapour at atmospheric pressure.
Which of these statements is/are correct?
questions.a: II and III only
o: II and III only
I and II only
I and III only
I, II and III

questions.q: True or false? 'The interparticle attraction in a liquid is slightly weaker than in a solid.' Give your verdict and one observation from the chapter that supports it.
questions.a: True. You can move a finger through water without breaking or cutting it permanently, which cannot be done with a solid; the water is only displaced for a moment and closes back when the finger is removed, so its attraction is weaker than in a solid but still strong enough to keep the particles close together.
s: Gives the verdict: True
Gives the finger observation: a finger moves through water without cutting it permanently, unlike a solid, and the water closes back

questions.q:
Washed clothes are hung out to dry on a cool morning in Shillong. The water in them never comes near its boiling point, yet the clothes are dry by evening.
(a) Name the process by which the water leaves the clothes.
(b) Give two ways in which this process differs from what happens in a pan of boiling water.
questions.a: (a) Evaporation. (b) Evaporation is slow, while at the boiling point vapour forms very fast; and evaporation happens only at the surface, while at the boiling point vapour also forms within the liquid, seen as bubbles.
s: (a) Names evaporation
(b) Gives both differences: slow versus very fast, and only at the surface versus also within the liquid

questions.q: Suman says, 'The big bubbles that rise all through water while it is boiling are just bubbles of air.' Check her claim using the chapter: (a) say what these bubbles are, (b) explain why they form inside the liquid at the boiling point, and (c) give your verdict.
questions.a: (a) They are vapour: water that has turned into the gaseous state. (b) At the boiling point the particles move so vigorously that they move apart, the attraction between them decreases and they escape from the liquid; vapour then forms very fast, not only at the surface but also within the liquid, which is seen as bubbles. (c) Her claim is wrong: the chapter explains the bubbling at the boiling point as vapour forming inside the liquid.
s: (a) The bubbles are vapour (the gaseous state of water)
(b) Particles move apart, attraction decreases and they escape, so vapour forms fast within the liquid
(c) Verdict: the claim is wrong

questions.q:
500 mL of water poured into three clean containers of different shapes takes a new shape each time but always measures 500 mL. Three students explain why.
Arun: 'Water particles have no attraction between them, so they spread anywhere.'
Bina: 'Water particles are held in fixed positions; the whole layer of water just bends to fit the container.'
Charu: 'Water particles can move freely, but only within a limited space, because their attraction is slightly weaker than in solids but still strong enough to keep them close together.'
(a) Which observation shows that Arun is wrong?
(b) Which observation from the chapter shows that Bina is wrong?
(c) Whose explanation matches the chapter?
(d) Use that explanation to say why the water takes the shape of each container.
(e) Use it to say why the volume stays at 500 mL.
questions.a: (a) The water keeps a definite volume of 500 mL in every container; it does not spread out to fill all the space, as a gas such as smoke does in a gas jar. (b) A finger can be moved through water without cutting it permanently, which cannot be done with a solid, so the particles are not held in fixed positions. (c) Charu's. (d) The particles are free to move, so the water flows and takes the shape of whatever container it is in. (e) The particles can move only within a limited space and the attraction keeps them close together, so the volume stays the same.
s: (a) Water keeps its 500 mL volume and does not spread to fill the space like a gas
(b) A finger moves through water without cutting it permanently, so its particles are not fixed
(c) Charu's explanation
(d) Particles are free to move, so the water takes the container's shape
(e) Particles move only within a limited space and stay close, so the volume is fixed

questions.q:
A Class 8 group in Amritsar measures 300 mL of water in a clean measuring jug. They pour it into a clean, dry tall bottle, then into a clean, dry round bowl, then into a clean, dry flat tray, and after each pour they tip it back into the jug to read the volume: 300 mL, 300 mL and 300 mL. Next, a student slowly draws a finger across the water in the tray and watches the water close up behind it. Finally, she puts an iron key into each of the three empty, dry containers in turn.
(a) What happens to the shape of the water in each container?
(b) What does the reading of 300 mL every time show about liquids?
(c) What does the finger observation show about the attraction between water particles, compared with a solid?
(d) The key keeps the same shape in all three containers. Using particles, explain why the key and the water behave differently.
questions.a: (a) The water takes the shape of each container it is poured into: tall in the bottle, round in the bowl, a flat layer in the tray. (b) Liquids have a definite (fixed) volume. (c) The attraction between water particles is slightly weaker than in a solid, so the finger can pass through without cutting the water permanently, but it is still strong enough to keep the particles close together, so the water closes up again. (d) In the key (a solid) the particles are tightly packed and held in fixed positions by very strong attraction, so it keeps its shape; in water the particles are free to move within a limited space, so it takes the container's shape.
s: (a) The water takes the shape of each container
(b) Liquids have a definite volume
(c) Attraction is slightly weaker than in a solid but still strong enough to keep particles close
(d) Key: particles fixed by very strong attraction; water: particles free to move within a limited space

questions.q:
Ramya heats a pan of water on a stove in her home in Kochi until it starts boiling. Answer each part in one line, using the particles of water.
(a) What happens to the movement of the water particles as the heating continues?
(b) What happens to the distance between the particles and to the attraction between them?
(c) What do the particles finally do when the water reaches its boiling point?
(d) What is the temperature at which a liquid boils and turns into vapour at atmospheric pressure called?
questions.a: (a) It becomes more and more vigorous. (b) The particles move apart from each other, so the interparticle attraction decreases. (c) They escape from the liquid, and the liquid is converted into vapour (the gaseous state). (d) Its boiling point.
s: (a) The movement becomes more vigorous
(b) The particles move apart and the attraction decreases
(c) The particles escape and the water turns into vapour
(d) The boiling point

questions.q: Why does the chapter group liquids and gases together as fluids?
questions.a: Both flow and do not retain a fixed shape
o: Both flow and do not retain a fixed shape
Both keep a fixed volume in every container
Both have particles held in fixed positions
Both have very strong interparticle attraction

questions.q: Violet iodine vapour, formed from solid iodine kept in a closed gas jar, spreads through the whole jar. Which other observation in the chapter shows the same property of gases?
questions.a: Smoke from one gas jar spreading to fill all of a second gas jar placed over it
o: Smoke from one gas jar spreading to fill all of a second gas jar placed over it
Water keeping the same 200 mL volume in three containers of different shapes
A finger moving through a dish of water without cutting it permanently
Sugar disappearing from view when it is stirred into a glass of water

questions.q:
Match each item in Column I with what it shows or is, in Column II.
Column I: 1. Smoke let into an empty gas jar fills the whole jar; 2. Smoke takes the shape of the jar it is in; 3. Tiny smoke specks are seen moving about; 4. The attraction between gas particles.
Column II: A. invisible gas particles keep hitting them; B. gases have no fixed volume; C. negligible; D. gases have no fixed shape.

Assertion (A): In the gas-jar activity, the tiny smoke specks are seen moving about inside the jar.
Reason (R): Gases do not have a fixed volume.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

questions.q: Give two reasons, in terms of particles, why gases have no fixed shape and no fixed volume.
questions.a: (1) The particles of a gas move freely in all directions. (2) The interparticle attractions between gas particles are negligible, so nothing holds them together and the gas spreads to occupy all the space available.
s: Gas particles move freely in all directions
The interparticle attraction between gas particles is negligible

questions.q:
Kabir says, 'If the particles of smoky air attracted each other as strongly as the particles of a solid do, the smoke let into Gas Jar B would still spread to fill the whole jar.'
(a) Is Kabir right?
(b) Give the reason, using the chapter.
questions.a: (a) No. (b) Attraction as strong as in a solid would hold the particles close together in fixed positions, giving a definite shape and volume, so the smoky air would not spread out. A gas fills the whole jar only because its particles move freely in all directions and the attraction between them is negligible.
s: (a) No, he is not right
(b) Strong attraction would hold the particles together; a gas spreads only because its attraction is negligible and its particles move freely

questions.q:
Say whether each of these is a fluid or not, and give a one-line reason.
(a) Milk in a glass
(b) The air inside a football
(c) An iron nail
questions.a: (a) A fluid: milk is a liquid, which flows and takes the shape of its container. (b) A fluid: air is a gas, which flows and takes the shape of its container. (c) Not a fluid: an iron nail is a solid, which does not flow and keeps a definite shape.
s: (a) Milk is a fluid, being a liquid that flows
(b) Air is a fluid, being a gas that flows
(c) The iron nail is not a fluid, being a solid with a fixed shape

questions.q: Using the particle picture in the chapter, explain why smoky air let into an open bowl does not stay in the bowl as a layer, the way water poured into the same bowl does.
questions.a: The particles of a gas move freely in all directions and the attraction between them is negligible, so a gas tends to occupy all the space available to it. In an open bowl the available space includes the room above, so the smoky air spreads out of the bowl. The particles of water are kept close together by attraction and can move only within a limited space, so water has a definite volume and stays in the bowl as a layer.
s: Gas particles move freely in all directions with negligible attraction
So the gas occupies all the available space and spreads out of the open bowl
Water particles are held close and move only within a limited space, so it has a definite volume and stays

questions.q:
Liquids and gases are both fluids, yet they behave differently. Differentiate between a liquid and a gas under these five heads.
(a) What they have in common that makes both of them fluids
(b) Volume
(c) Interparticle attraction
(d) Movement of particles
(e) One observation from the chapter's activities that shows the difference in volume
questions.a: (a) Both flow and do not retain a fixed shape. (b) A liquid has a definite volume; a gas has no fixed volume and occupies the entire space available. (c) In a liquid the attraction is slightly weaker than in a solid but strong enough to keep the particles close together; in a gas it is negligible. (d) Liquid particles move freely but only within a limited space; gas particles move freely in all directions. (e) Water stayed at 200 mL in three containers of different shapes, while smoke spread to fill the whole of Gas Jar B.
s: (a) Both flow and do not retain a fixed shape
(b) Liquid: definite volume; gas: no fixed volume, fills the space
(c) Liquid: attraction strong enough to keep particles close; gas: negligible
(d) Liquid: movement within a limited space; gas: free movement in all directions
(e) Water kept its volume in different containers while smoke filled the whole gas jar

questions.q: Rohit writes in his notebook: 'Gases are not really matter, because we cannot see them and they do not even have a fixed shape.' Evaluate his claim. Give your verdict, say how the chapter treats gases, and support your answer with two pieces of evidence from the chapter's activities.
questions.a: Verdict: the claim is wrong. The chapter treats the gaseous state as one of the three states of matter: a gas is made of particles that move freely in all directions with negligible attraction, which is why it has no fixed shape. Evidence 1: in the gas-jar activity the smoke specks are seen moving because they are constantly hit by invisible gas particles, so gas particles exist even though we cannot see them. Evidence 2: air trapped in a sealed syringe takes up space: pushing the plunger only brings its particles closer and reduces its volume, and the plunger moves back when released.
s: Verdict: the claim is wrong
The chapter treats gas as a state of matter made of freely moving particles with negligible attraction
Evidence: smoke specks move because invisible gas particles keep hitting them
Evidence: trapped air in a sealed syringe takes up space; it can be squeezed and pushes the plunger back

questions.q: Deepa pulls the plunger of a syringe without a needle fully outwards, closes the open end tightly with her thumb and slowly pushes the plunger inwards. What does she observe?
questions.a: The volume of the air inside the syringe decreases
o: The volume of the air inside the syringe decreases
The volume of the air inside stays exactly the same
The air inside the syringe turns into water drops
The plunger cannot be moved inwards at all

questions.q: When the syringe activity is repeated with different substances, which of these is found to be practically incompressible?
questions.a: Water
o: Water
Air
Smoky air
Iodine vapour

questions.q: In a dissolving activity, the water level in a vessel is marked at 120 mL (level A). Sugar is added and the new level is 128 mL (level B). After stirring until all the sugar dissolves, the level is 125 mL (level C). By how much did the level fall when the sugar dissolved?
questions.a: 3 mL
o: 3 mL
5 mL
8 mL
125 mL

questions.q:
Consider these statements.
I. If you stop pushing the plunger of a sealed, air-filled syringe, the air particles spread out and the plunger moves back to its original position.
II. Water in a sealed syringe can be squeezed to half its volume by pushing the plunger hard.
III. Sand stirred into water dissolves, and its particles fill the spaces between the water particles.
Which of these statements is/are correct?
questions.a: I only
o: I only
I and II only
I and III only
II and III only

questions.q: True or false? 'The particles of a gas have very little space between them, which is why the air in a sealed syringe cannot be pushed into a smaller volume.' Give your verdict and the correct idea.
questions.a: False. Gas particles have a lot of space between them in their natural state. Pushing the plunger forces them closer, so the volume of the air in the sealed syringe does decrease.
s: Gives the verdict: False
Corrects it: gas particles have a lot of space between them, so the trapped air can be compressed into a smaller volume

questions.q:
(a) What does the chapter say is present in the spaces between the particles of a solid?
(b) Are the particles of a solid packed so closely that no space at all is left between them?
questions.a: (a) Nothing at all: the spaces are not filled with air. (b) No. Despite close packing, some space is still left between the particles of a solid.
s: (a) Nothing at all, not air
(b) No, some space is left between the particles despite close packing

questions.q:
Answer briefly.
(a) Does sand dissolve in water?
(b) What happens to the water level when sand is added to water and stirred?
(c) Why is the result different when sugar is used instead?
questions.a: (a) No, sand is insoluble in water. (b) The sand particles settle down and occupy their own space in the container, so the total volume increases and the level stays up. (c) Sugar dissolves: its particles occupy the spaces between the water particles, so after dissolving the level comes down below the level marked just after the sugar was added.
s: (a) No, sand does not dissolve
(b) Sand settles and takes up its own space, so the volume increases
(c) Dissolved sugar particles occupy the spaces between water particles, so the level falls

questions.q: Lata says, 'Air in a sealed syringe can be squeezed but water cannot, so there must be no spaces at all between water particles.' Check her claim: say what is right in it, what is wrong, and give your verdict.
questions.a: Right: water is practically incompressible, so the spaces between its particles are much smaller than the large spaces between gas particles. Wrong: there are spaces between water particles. When sugar is dissolved, the volume of the solution is less than the sum of the volumes of the water and the sugar, because the dissolved sugar particles occupy spaces between the water particles. Verdict: partly right; the spaces in water are small, not absent.
s: Right part: water is practically incompressible, so its spaces are much smaller than in a gas
Wrong part: the sugar activity shows spaces between water particles that dissolved particles occupy
Verdict: partly right; the spaces are small, not absent

questions.q:
A group in Jodhpur fills four vessels with water to the 100 mL mark and adds a different solid to each. They read the level just after adding the solid and again after stirring well.
Sugar: 106 mL, then 103 mL. Common salt: 104 mL, then 102 mL. Sand: 107 mL, then 107 mL. Stone pieces: 105 mL, then 105 mL.
(a) Which two solids dissolved? How can you tell from the readings?
(b) By how many mL did the level fall for each of these two solids?
(c) Why does the level fall when a solid dissolves?
(d) Why did the level stay up for sand and stone pieces?
(e) A student says, 'The volume of a solution is always the sum of the volumes of the water and the solid added.' Do the sugar readings support this? Use the numbers.
questions.a: (a) Sugar and common salt: only for these did the level fall after stirring. (b) Sugar: 106 - 103 = 3 mL; common salt: 104 - 102 = 2 mL. (c) The particles of the dissolved solid occupy the spaces between the water particles, so the solution takes up less room than the water and the solid did separately. (d) Sand and stone are insoluble; their particles settle down and occupy their own space in the vessel, so the total volume increases and stays up. (e) No. The water and the sugar together gave 106 mL just after adding, but the solution measures only 103 mL, which is less than the sum.
s: (a) Sugar and common salt, because their levels fell after stirring
(b) 3 mL for sugar and 2 mL for common salt
(c) Dissolved particles occupy the spaces between water particles
(d) Insoluble solids settle and occupy their own space, so the volume stays up
(e) No: the solution is 103 mL, less than the 106 mL sum

questions.q:
A Class 8 group in Bhubaneswar fills a 60 mL syringe (without a needle) with air and seals the open end with a thumb. As they push the plunger harder and harder, the reading falls from 60 mL to 45 mL and then to 35 mL. When they let go, the plunger moves back to 60 mL. They repeat the test with the same syringe completely filled with water: however hard they push, the reading stays at 60 mL. One student now wants to make a model 'shock absorber' from a sealed syringe that gives way a little when pressed and springs back when released.
(a) By how many mL did the volume of the air decrease at the hardest push?
(b) Why could the air be squeezed into a smaller volume?
(c) Why did the plunger return to 60 mL when they let go?
(d) Should the student fill her shock absorber with air or with water? Justify using the readings.
questions.a: (a) 60 - 35 = 25 mL. (b) The particles of a gas have a lot of space between them, and pushing the plunger (applying external pressure) reduces this space by forcing the particles closer. (c) When the push stops, the gas particles spread out again, so the plunger moves back to its original position. (d) Air: the air readings show it gives way under a push (60 to 35 mL) and springs back to 60 mL, while water stayed at 60 mL because it is practically incompressible, so a water-filled syringe would not give way at all.
s: (a) 25 mL
(b) Gas particles have a lot of space between them, which pressure reduces
(c) The gas particles spread out again when the push stops
(d) Chooses air: it compresses and springs back, while water is practically incompressible

questions.q: Neel drops a few grains of potassium permanganate into a glass tumbler of water and does not stir it. What does he see?
questions.a: Pink streaks spread out from the grains at first, and later the whole of the water becomes uniformly pink
o: Pink streaks spread out from the grains at first, and later the whole of the water becomes uniformly pink
The whole of the water turns pink at once, and later the colour gathers back around the grains
Nothing happens at all until the water is stirred well with a spoon or a glass rod
The pink colour stays only around the grains, however long he waits beside the glass

questions.q: Reena drops an equal small grain of potassium permanganate into each of three tumblers: one of hot water, one of water at room temperature and one of ice-cold water. In which order does the colour spread, from the fastest to the slowest?
questions.a: Hot water, room-temperature water, ice-cold water
o: Hot water, room-temperature water, ice-cold water
Ice-cold water, room-temperature water, hot water
Room-temperature water, hot water, ice-cold water
All three spread at the same speed

questions.q:
Match each observation or case in Column I with the explanation in Column II.
Column I: 1. Pink colour slowly spreads through still water from a potassium permanganate grain; 2. The colour spreads fastest in hot water; 3. A grain of sand does not spread through water; 4. The particles of a solid, whose thermal energy is low.
Column II: A. its particles are held together too strongly for water particles to pull them out; B. are restricted to small vibrations; C. water particles are in constant motion and hit the permanganate particles; D. the movement of particles increases when heat is provided.

Assertion (A): The thermal energy of particles has no effect on whether a substance is a solid, a liquid or a gas.
Reason (R): The strength of the attraction between particles depends on the distance between them, which in turn depends on their thermal energy.
questions.a: A is false but R is true.
o: A is false but R is true.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.

questions.q:
Ira sprays perfume near the door of her closed classroom.
(a) Who will smell it first: a student sitting near the door or one at the far end of the room?
(b) Why does the smell later reach the far end of the room too?
questions.a: (a) The student sitting near the door. (b) The particles of air are constantly moving; they hit the particles of the perfume and help them spread through the whole room.
s: (a) The student near the door
(b) Constantly moving air particles hit the perfume particles and spread them through the room

questions.q: True or false? 'When a solid reaches its melting point, the distance between its particles increases only slightly, yet this is enough for the particles to move around within a limited space.' Give your verdict and the reason.
questions.a: True. At the melting point the thermal energy overcomes the attractive forces enough for the particles to leave their fixed positions. The interparticle distance increases only slightly, but this reduces the strength of the attractive forces to a level that lets the particles move around, though still within a limited space.
s: Gives the verdict: True
Reason: the slight increase in distance weakens the attraction enough for the particles to move around within a limited space

questions.a: (a) Gas. (b) Solid. (c) Liquid.
s: (a) Gas
(b) Solid
(c) Liquid

questions.q: 'It is the thermal energy of the particles that determines the physical state of matter.' Justify this statement in five points, using the chapter's ideas about interparticle attraction, the solid state, the melting point, the gaseous state and the effect of heat on the movement of particles.
questions.a: (1) The strength of the attraction between particles depends on the distance between them, which in turn depends on their thermal energy. (2) In a solid the thermal energy of the particles is low, so they stay close together with strong attraction and can only vibrate. (3) At the melting point the thermal energy overcomes the attractive forces enough for the particles to leave their fixed positions; the distance increases slightly and they move within a limited space, so the solid becomes a liquid. (4) In the gaseous state the particles have enough energy to overcome the attraction and move freely in all directions. (5) Heat speeds up particles: potassium permanganate spreads fastest in hot water and slowest in ice-cold water, showing that particle movement increases when heat is provided.
s: Attraction depends on distance, which depends on thermal energy
Solid: low thermal energy, particles close with strong attraction, only vibrate
Melting point: thermal energy overcomes attraction, particles leave fixed positions and move within a limited space
Gas: enough energy to overcome attraction, particles move freely in all directions
Evidence: permanganate spreads fastest in hot water, so movement increases with heat

questions.q:
A dyeing workshop in Bagru, Rajasthan, drops the same amount of a dye powder that dissolves in water into two identical vats of still water, without stirring. In Vat 1, with water at 60 °C, the colour is even all through the vat after 12 minutes. In Vat 2, with water at 20 °C, it takes 48 minutes. Heating a vat to 60 °C uses Rs 30 of fuel, while Vat 2 costs nothing extra. Today the cloth must be dipped within 30 minutes of adding the dye.
(a) In which vat are the water particles moving faster?
(b) How many times as long does Vat 2 take as Vat 1?
(c) Explain how the dye reaches every part of the vat without any stirring.
(d) Which vat should the workshop use today, and what does that choice cost? Justify with the times.
questions.a: (a) Vat 1, the hot water: water particles move faster when they have more heat energy. (b) 48 / 12 = 4 times as long. (c) The water particles are in constant motion; they pull particles of the dye out of the powder and then hit them, so the dye particles get spread throughout the water. (d) Vat 1, at a fuel cost of Rs 30: it is ready in 12 minutes, within the 30-minute limit, while Vat 2 needs 48 minutes and would not be ready in time.
s: (a) Vat 1, the hot water
(b) 4 times as long
(c) Moving water particles pull dye particles out of the powder and hit them so they spread
(d) Vat 1 for Rs 30, because 12 minutes is within 30 minutes and 48 minutes is not

questions.q:
Two identical closed rooms have their windows shut and fans off. Room P is at 18 °C on a winter morning and Room Q is at 32 °C on a summer afternoon. An incense stick is lit in one corner of each room.
(a) Where in each room is the fragrance felt first?
(b) Which particles help the fragrance spread through the room, and how?
(c) Predict in which room the fragrance will reach the far corner sooner.
(d) Give the reason for your prediction from the chapter.
questions.a: (a) Near the incense stick, in the corner where it is lit. (b) The particles of air: they are constantly moving and hit the particles of the fragrance, helping them spread through the room. (c) Room Q, the warmer room. (d) The movement of particles increases when heat is provided, as the potassium permanganate activity showed for water, so the warmer air particles move faster and spread the fragrance sooner.
s: (a) Near the incense stick first
(b) Constantly moving air particles hit the fragrance particles and spread them
(c) Room Q, the warmer room
(d) Particle movement increases with heat, so the warmer air spreads the fragrance faster
